title: Descartes Colloquium: Herder's Nondualism / The Rise of Women: Making of a Modern Myth
speaker: Vicki A. Spencer (University of Auckland / Senior Descartes Centre Fellow) and Annelien de Dijn (Utrecht University)
location: Johanna Hudig building, room 1.27 (Alex Brenninkmeijer room), entrance Kromme Nieuwegracht 47E
description: Descartes Centre Colloquium on history & philosophy of science (replaces the UPAC Colloquium this week). Two talks. Hybrid; e-mail dc-colloquium@uu.nl for the Teams link.
abstract:
Vicki A. Spencer, "Herder's Nondualism":
The idea that Herder is an anti-dualist in contradistinction to the earlier dismissal of his work as fundamentally contradictory is now widely accepted in Herder scholarship. My early work also contributed to this rethinking of Herder's importance in the history of philosophy. Yet due to the way recent scholarship has applied the term 'anti-dualist' to thinkers like Leibniz, I argue in this paper that Herder is more appropriately seen as a nondualist. For Herder, the mind and body, reason and emotion, literal and figurative language, and nature and culture do not exist in a hierarchical relationship in which the mind, reason, literal language, and culture are deemed to have greater validity than their apparent opposites. Critiques of dichotomous thinking have enjoyed increased interest in Western thinking since Derrida's deconstruction of dualisms, and they are a common feature of an array of feminist positions. But Herder does not only criticize dualistic thinking or invert these dichotomies. His holistic philosophy challenges the very existence of separate, mutually exclusive categories and fixed categories and the law of non-contradiction in analytical philosophy by providing a positive nondualist alternative that blurs the boundaries of these categories by virtue of their interaction and mutual dependency. It thus differs from Leibniz's anti-dualist position which challenges the idea that reality is composed of fundamentally distinct entities or substances, like the mind and the body, but denies interaction between them. And contra Michael Forster, who claims Herder still possessed a dualist philosophy of the mind in the early 1770s and largely owes his anti-dualism to his reading of Spinoza, I argue that Herder's nondualism was firmly established in his award-winning 1772 Treatise on the Origin of Language.

Annelien de Dijn, "The Rise of Women: Making of a Modern Myth":
Today, modernity and gender equality are often seen as intimately entwined. Modernisation is held to promote equality between men and women by transforming traditional social structures and expanding women's opportunities. Where does this idea come from? And why does it have such a durable hold over our collective imagination, despite all evidence to the contrary? In this paper, I aim to answer these questions by examining the contribution of modern scholarship, notably within the social sciences, to the invention and development of this modern myth. The claim that modernisation leads to gender equality, I show, was first developed by the legal historian Henry Maine in the context of Victorian debates about prehistory. Through Maine's influence on pioneering sociologists such as Ferdinand Tönnies, Max Weber and Emile Durkheim, it subsequently became a key component of continental sociology. In the second half of the twentieth century, modernisation theorists continued to enthusiastically embrace this narrative, despite growing criticism by feminist scholars. In order to understand why this was the case, we need to see that the modernization narrative served multiple, and sometimes contradictory, political uses. Thus, this paper throws new light on the genealogy of one of modernity's most cherished myths.
